nodes.label: Hattusili I
nodes.full: A king of Kussara who made Hattusa his seat and took the name Hattusili, 'man of Hattusa', in defiance of Anitta's curse. His Annals tell of campaigns across the Taurus into Syria, where he destroyed Alalakh and raided Hashshu and Hahhum. His Testament, disowning one heir and adopting his grandson Mursili, is the first Hittite state paper on the succession.
nodes.src: Annals of Hattusili I (CTH 4); Testament of Hattusili I (CTH 6); Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

nodes.label: Mursili I
nodes.full: Mursili finished the destruction of Aleppo's kingdom of Yamhad and, in about 1595 BC, marched down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon, ending the dynasty of Hammurabi. He then withdrew with his spoils and was murdered at home by his brother-in-law Hantili and Zidanta. The kingdom's reach fell away as quickly as it had been won.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19); Babylonian Chronicle of Early Kings; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Age of murders
nodes.full: Telipinu's later edict lists the murders in the royal house: Mursili by Hantili and Zidanta, Zidanta by his own son Ammuna, and so on down to the overthrow of Huzziya. In these two generations Kizzuwatna broke away, Hurrian power grew in Syria, and the Kaska pressed on the north.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Telipinu
nodes.full: Telipinu, who took the throne from Huzziya I, rebuilt the state on law rather than force, by clear rules of succession, a council of nobles and a ban on killing royal kin without trial. He made a treaty with Isputahsu of Kizzuwatna. The Old Kingdom ends in his edict, not his death.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19); Treaty of Telipinu with Isputahsu (CTH 21).

nodes.label: Tudhaliya I/II
nodes.full: After a thin century, Tudhaliya (the I/II of the modern numbering) beat the Assuwa league in the west, retook Kizzuwatna and campaigned in Syria. His successor Arnuwanda I and his queen Asmunikal faced the Kaska in the north, to the point that the court worked from Sapinuwa. A well-known prayer of the pair confesses the loss of temples in the Kaska raids.
nodes.src: Annals of Tudhaliya I/II (CTH 142); Prayer of Arnuwanda and Asmunikal (CTH 375); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Suppiluliuma I
nodes.full: The son of Tudhaliya III restored Hattusa, then in the Syrian War destroyed Mitanni as a great power, took Carchemish and Aleppo, and installed sons as viceroys there. He made treaties with kings from Ugarit to Amurru. His reign brought the Hittites into the diplomacy of the Amarna Age, and ended in a plague that killed him and his heir.
nodes.src: Deeds of Suppiluliuma (CTH 40), written by his son Mursili II; Treaty with Shattiwaza (CTH 51); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Mursili II
nodes.full: Mursili inherited a plague-struck realm and revolts on every border. In ten years' annals and later campaigns he crushed Arzawa, reduced the Kaska and restored the Syrian provinces. He also wrote, in his prayers, one of the earliest personal laments in literature, begging the gods to end the pestilence.
nodes.src: Ten-Year Annals of Mursili II (CTH 61); Plague Prayers (CTH 378); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Muwatalli II
nodes.full: Muwatalli II moved the royal seat and the gods to Tarhuntassa in the south, leaving his brother Hattusili in the north as governor of the Upper Land. He fought Ramesses II to a standstill at Kadesh in 1274 BC and made a treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa. In his last years the kingdom was held together by his strong brother and a weak heir.
nodes.src: Kadesh reliefs and Poem of Pentaur; Treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa (CTH 76); Apology of Hattusili III (CTH 81); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Urhi-Teshub
nodes.full: Muwatalli's son by a concubine took the throne as Mursili III and brought the court back to Hattusa. After seven years his uncle Hattusili, who had been his loyal general, moved against him. Urhi-Teshub was exiled to Syria and later turned up in Egypt, where he plotted his return.
nodes.src: Apology of Hattusili III (CTH 81); letters from the Hattusa archive.

nodes.label: Hattusili III, Puduhepa
nodes.full: Hattusili, a younger son who had been a sickly child and a successful governor, took the throne in a coup and justified it in a long apology. With his queen Puduhepa, daughter of a priest of Kizzuwatna, he ruled as a pair — she wrote her own letters and sealed treaties — and he made the peace with Egypt in 1259 BC.
nodes.src: Apology of Hattusili III (CTH 81); Treaty of Hattusili III and Ramesses II (CTH 91); Puduhepa's letters and seals.

nodes.label: Tudhaliya IV
nodes.full: Tudhaliya IV enlarged Hattusa with a new Upper City of temples, built the chamber sanctuaries at Yazılıkaya, and faced a stronger Assyria. He was beaten by Assyria at Nihriya, barred Assyrian merchants from the sea route to Ahhiyawa, and quarrelled with his cousin Kurunta of Tarhuntassa. Egypt's friendship and the empire's grain supply were by then both shaky.
nodes.src: Tudhaliya IV's inscriptions (Yazılıkaya, Yalburt); Bronze tablet of Kurunta (CTH 106); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: The last kings
nodes.full: Arnuwanda III reigned briefly, and his brother Suppiluliuma II is the last known Great King. His inscriptions at the Nişantaş and in Chamber 2 at Yerkapı boast of campaigns in the south and of sea battles against Alashiya. Within a few years the capital was being emptied of its archives and elite, and the king disappears from the record.
nodes.src: Nişantaş inscription of Suppiluliuma II; Chamber 2 at Yerkapı; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Viceroys of Carchemish
nodes.full: Suppiluliuma installed his son Piyassili (Sharri-Kushuh) as king in Carchemish to run the Syrian provinces for the empire. His line, which included Talmi-Teshub and Kuzi-Teshub, held authority over Aleppo, Ugarit and Amurru. After Hattusa fell, the dynasty stayed on as the Great Kings of Carchemish.
nodes.src: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Shattiwaza (CTH 51); the archives of Emar and Ugarit; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Tarhuntassa, Kurunta
nodes.full: Muwatalli's southern seat of Tarhuntassa was made a kingdom for his son Kurunta, whose treaty with Tudhaliya IV on a bronze tablet was found at Hattusa in 1986. Kurunta's seal appears even as a Great King's, which may mean he held the throne briefly. The kingdom's location is still a matter of debate.
nodes.src: Bronze tablet from Hattusa (CTH 106; found 1986); Kurunta sealings; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Hattusili in Syria
nodes.full: Hattusili took his army over the Taurus and into northern Syria, destroying Alalakh (Tell Atchana) and crossing the Euphrates, while the kingdom of Yamhad at Aleppo resisted. His Annals record the campaigns, and the archaeological destruction of Alalakh VII fits with them. It was the first Hittite war of conquest outside Anatolia.
nodes.src: Annals of Hattusili I (CTH 4); Woolley's Alalakh excavations (1937–49).

nodes.label: Sack of Babylon
nodes.full: Mursili's army marched from Aleppo down the Euphrates to Babylon, which fell in a single stroke, and its dynasty of Hammurabi ended. The Hittites carried off the cult statues of Marduk and his consort and did not stay. It is the longest raid of the Old Kingdom, and the one that opened the door for the Kassites.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19), §9; Babylonian Chronicle of Early Kings; Chronicle of Telipinu.

nodes.label: Kaska raids
nodes.full: The mountain peoples of the Pontic range, who lived without kings, raided the Hittite heartland across the generations, taking sacred cities such as Nerik and burning other places. Texts of Arnuwanda I and Suppiluliuma tell of Hattusa itself in danger and of the king going out each spring to fight them. The frontier was never settled for the empire's whole life.
nodes.src: Prayer of Arnuwanda and Asmunikal (CTH 375); Deeds of Suppiluliuma; Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Assuwa league
nodes.full: Tudhaliya I/II defeated a league of twenty-two western lands led by Assuwa, which included Wilusa (Troy) and Taruisa, and took many captives back to Hattusa. It is the first Hittite contact with the Aegean world and the earliest written record of the Wilusa that Greek poets would call Ilios.
nodes.src: Annals of Tudhaliya I/II (CTH 142).

nodes.label: Fall of Mitanni
nodes.full: Suppiluliuma's first Syrian campaign was followed by a long war in which he crossed the Euphrates, took Carchemish after a siege and made Mitanni's rival, the pretender Shattiwaza, his son-in-law and vassal. Mitanni, the great power of Syria, was reduced to a client state between Hatti and rising Assyria.
nodes.src: Deeds of Suppiluliuma (CTH 40); Treaty with Shattiwaza (CTH 51).

nodes.label: War on Arzawa
nodes.full: Mursili II marched against Uhhazitis of Arzawa in his third year, took the capital Apasa, and the king fled overseas. The Arzawa kingdom was divided into the vassal states of Mira, Seha River Land and Hapalla. For the first time, the whole west was in Hittite hands.
nodes.src: Annals of Mursili II (CTH 61); Treaty with Kupanta-Kurunta of Mira.

nodes.label: Kadesh
nodes.full: Muwatalli II and Ramesses II met at Kadesh on the Orontes with armies of tens of thousands of men and thousands of chariots by the Egyptian accounts. Ramesses was ambushed and rescued, and left claiming victory on temple walls across Egypt; the Hittites held Kadesh and Amurru. It is the best-documented ancient battle and a draw.
nodes.src: Egyptian Poem of Pentaur and Bulletin; Kadesh reliefs at Abu Simbel and Karnak; Hittite references in the Apology (CTH 81).

nodes.label: Nihriya
nodes.full: Tudhaliya IV met the Assyrian Tukulti-Ninurta I in the upper Tigris lands and lost. The Assyrian king calls the Hittite ruler 'the Hatti king' and boasts of 28,800 captives. The defeat meant the loss of the eastern buffer and of a key trade axis.
nodes.src: Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta (Middle Assyrian); Hittite letters on the embargo (CTH 105); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: End of Hattusa
nodes.full: Hattusa was gradually emptied of its royal family, officials and archives within a few decades, and then burned, probably after the state had left. For a long time the fire was read as a conquest by outsiders; excavators now see a managed abandonment followed by the burning of the palace and temples. What drove the elite out is debated: drought, famine, revolts and external enemies are all proposed.
nodes.src: Jürgen Seeher, Hattusha Guide (2006); Theo van den Hout in the Cambridge history volume; Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Edict of Telipinu
nodes.full: Telipinu's decree begins with history, tells the sequence of murders from Hattusili to Huzziya, and ends with a law: the throne passes to the eldest son of the first rank, and failing that the husband of the eldest daughter, and blood must not be shed within the royal house without trial by the assembly. The pankus of nobles was given a part in judging the king's kin.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19), ed. Inge Hoffmann (1984).

nodes.label: Hittite Laws
nodes.full: Two tablets of about two hundred clauses fix compensation for injury, theft, marriage, land service and the prices of cattle and work. The rule is restitution, not retaliation: the bodily harm of the old 'eye for an eye' is turned into a payment of silver. Later copies update the penalties downward.
nodes.src: The Hittite Laws (CTH 291–292), ed. Harry Hoffner, The Laws of the Hittites (1997).

nodes.label: Vassal treaty form
nodes.full: The treaties with Ugarit, Amurru, Mira, Wilusa, Mitanni and Kizzuwatna share a form: a preamble with the Great King's titles, a prologue recounting past favours, stipulations of loyalty and tribute, divine witnesses, and blessings and curses. The Hittite vassal treaty is the best-known template of the diplomatic world, and scholars since Mendenhall have compared its form with biblical covenant texts.
nodes.src: Treaties collected in CTH 40–76; Gary Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts (1996); George Mendenhall (1954) on the covenant parallel.

nodes.label: The pankus
nodes.full: The king ruled with the pankus, the assembly of nobles, and with a household of bodyguards, cupbearers, chief scribes and the chief of the wine. The queen, as tawananna, held a post in her own right with estates and a staff; the heir was named the tuhkanti. The state was kin-based in structure, and kinsmen filled the major posts.
nodes.src: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19); Instructions for the palace staff (CTH 262–275); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Thousand gods
nodes.full: The state religion absorbed the gods of every people it ruled — Hattic, Hurrian, Luwian and Mesopotamian — and treaty texts call them 'the thousand gods of Hatti'. At the head stood the Storm God of Hatti and the Sun Goddess of Arinna, whom the queen served as priestess. Conquered gods were often brought to Hattusa and given offerings.
nodes.src: Treaty god-lists (CTH 40–76); Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994).

nodes.label: Plague prayers
nodes.full: Mursili prayed to the Storm God and to all the gods to end a plague which had lasted twenty years, asking what sin had brought it. Oracle inquiries traced it to a broken treaty oath and to neglected offerings to a river. Few texts of the ancient world show a ruler so exposed in his guilt.
nodes.src: Plague Prayers of Mursili II (CTH 378); Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002).

nodes.label: Oracles
nodes.full: Decisions about war, illness, temples and festivals were put to the gods through oracles: birds were watched, lots were drawn, sheep's livers read. Hundreds of oracle texts give a question and a yes or no answer, and are repeated by a second method to check it. The practice was a state procedure used to settle disputes, not a private superstition.
nodes.src: Oracle texts (CTH 560–582); Ada Taggar-Cohen, Hittite Priesthood (2006).

nodes.label: Hurrian gods
nodes.full: Puduhepa, from Kizzuwatna, brought the Hurrian pair Teshub and Hebat to the front rank. The Hurrian reform equated the Storm God of Hatti with Teshub and the Sun Goddess of Arinna with Hebat, and the royal family's rock sanctuary at Yazılıkaya shows them meeting at the head of the gods' procession.
nodes.src: Puduhepa's prayer to the Sun Goddess of Arinna (CTH 384); Haas 1994.

nodes.label: Walls of Hattusa
nodes.full: A ring of stone-footed walls, 6 kilometres long, enclosed the city and its Upper City, with gates guarded by carved lions, sphinxes and a warrior god. The Lion Gate and King's Gate sit among the best known monuments of Anatolia. Hattusa was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
nodes.src: Peter Neve and Jürgen Seeher, Boğazköy-Hattusa excavation reports (DAI, 1931–); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 377.

nodes.label: Yazılıkaya
nodes.full: In an open-air rock sanctuary outside the city, a long procession of gods and goddesses in relief files towards the meeting of Teshub and Hebat in Chamber A. In Chamber B, a smaller room, Tudhaliya IV is shown in the embrace of his protector god Sharruma, and a sword-god relief; the chamber may have served as the king's memorial. It is the great monument of Hittite religious art.
nodes.src: Kurt Bittel, Yazılıkaya (1975); Tudhaliya IV inscriptions at Yazılıkaya.

nodes.label: Great Temple
nodes.full: The temple of the Storm God of Hatti and the Sun Goddess of Arinna was the largest in the city, with a courtyard and cult room surrounded by storerooms in two or more storeys. It held the cult and the grain stores of the state gods. Such temple complexes formed a major part of the capital.
nodes.src: Peter Neve, Die Grabungen im Stadtgebiet von Boğazköy (Büyük Tempel, 1970s–1990s).

nodes.label: Alaca reliefs
nodes.full: At a major cult city north-east of Hattusa the gate was flanked by sphinxes and its walls carry orthostat reliefs of a king and queen before a bull, of musicians and acrobats, and of a hunt. The reliefs are among the main Hittite figurative works outside the capital and show a performance scene alongside ritual.
nodes.src: H. Z. Koşay and Mahmut Akok, Alaca Höyük excavation reports; Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara.

nodes.label: Inandık vase
nodes.full: A large cult vessel decorated with four reliefs showing a festival: a priest, libations, a sacred marriage, and musicians playing instruments including a lyre while acrobats perform. It is the best picture of music in an Old Hittite festival and was found in a temple at Inandıktepe.
nodes.src: Tahsin Özgüç, Inandıktepe: An Important Cult Center in the Old Hittite Period (1988).

nodes.label: Ullikummi
nodes.full: The Hurrian-Hittite epic of the stone giant Ullikummi, grown from a rock to challenge the gods and brought down when the old gods cut him from his base with the copper knife that once separated heaven from earth. It belongs to the Hurrian Kumarbi cycle of the kingship in heaven, whose succession myth is the closest known parallel to Hesiod's Theogony.
nodes.src: Song of Ullikummi (CTH 345); Hoffner, Hittite Myths (1998).

nodes.label: Royal annals
nodes.full: Hittite kings had their deeds written down year by year, the Annals of Hattusili I, Tudhaliya, Suppiluliuma and Mursili II among them. They give dates by campaigns and are structured as a narrative of cause and consequence, which makes them among the earliest true historiography of the ancient Near East. They are prized for naming enemies, motives and defeats.
nodes.src: Annals of Hattusili I (CTH 4); Deeds of Suppiluliuma (CTH 40); Annals of Mursili II (CTH 61).

nodes.label: Apology of Hattusili
nodes.full: Hattusili's long autobiographical text justifies his seizure of the throne, from his sickly boyhood through the goddess Ishtar's favour and loyal service to his nephew, to the day he took the crown. It is an early example of political self-justification that is also a personal narrative, meant to be read before the gods and the nobles.
nodes.src: Apology of Hattusili III (CTH 81), ed. Hans Otten (1981).

nodes.label: Kikkuli
nodes.full: The 'Master of Horses' Kikkuli, a man of Mitanni, wrote a tablet of 184 days of training for chariot horses, with timed exercise, feed, water and rest, in a text full of Indo-Aryan technical terms. It is the oldest surviving manual for the training of horses.
nodes.src: Kikkuli texts (CTH 284–285), ed. Annelies Kammenhuber (1961).

nodes.label: Tablet houses
nodes.full: More than 30,000 tablet fragments from Hattusa, in at least seven languages, include state treaties, letters, rituals, laws, oracle reports and literary texts in Hittite, Akkadian, Sumerian, Hattic, Hurrian, Luwian and Palaic. The archive is the main source on the Late Bronze Age Near East and the main means by which Hittite itself was deciphered, in 1915, by Bedřich Hrozný.
nodes.src: Boğazköy tablets (KBo, KUB); Bedřich Hrozný, 'Die Lösung des hethitischen Problems' (1915).

nodes.label: Rain-fed grain
nodes.full: The Hittite heartland lay on a rain-fed plateau, with a thin margin for good harvests. Hattusa's silos and the crown's grain pits stored barley and emmer against failure, and the king's household estates were organised partly to feed the cities. When harvests failed the state had to import grain from Egypt or from vassals like Ugarit.
nodes.src: Jürgen Seeher on the silo complexes of Hattusa; Hattusa archive letters on grain.

nodes.label: Silver and shekel
nodes.full: Prices, wages, fines and tribute were fixed in silver by weight, in shekels and minas, and goods were valued by it, though paid in kind. The Hittite Laws set the price of an ox, a sheep or a day's work in shekels. There was no coinage, and silver was the common medium across the Near East.
nodes.src: Hittite Laws (CTH 291–292); Hoffner 1997.

nodes.label: Deportees
nodes.full: Hittite kings brought tens of thousands of civilians from conquered lands — the NAM.RA, or 'deportees' — to settle as farmers, craftsmen and soldiers in the empire's heartland. The Annals of Mursili II give figures in the tens of thousands for the Arzawa campaigns alone. The policy fed the labour needs of the state and the army and mixed the peoples of Anatolia.
nodes.src: Annals of Mursili II (CTH 61); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Famine
nodes.full: Letters from Ugarit and Hattusa speak of famine in the land of Hatti, with the Hittite king asking for grain by ship from Ugarit and Egypt. Merneptah's Karnak inscription claims to have sent grain in ships 'to keep alive the land of Hatti'. The great state could not feed itself in its last decades.
nodes.src: Ugarit letters (RS 20.212, 18.147); Merneptah's Karnak inscription; Bryce 2005.

nodes.label: Postern tunnel
nodes.full: Beneath the great earthen rampart of the southern city, a corbelled stone tunnel about seventy metres long runs through the fortification, a postern that let troops sally from the walls. The rampart itself, with a stone-faced slope, is a distinctive Hittite defensive form.
nodes.src: Peter Neve, Boğazköy-Hattusa reports (Yerkapı, 1960s–70s).

nodes.label: Three-man chariot
nodes.full: The Hittites fought from heavy chariots with a crew of three — driver, spearman and shield-bearer — against the two-man Egyptian light chariot, and used them for shock. The Kadesh reliefs show them crowded at the ford. The chariot arm was the empire's main striking force.
nodes.src: Kadesh reliefs (Ramesseum, Abu Simbel); Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

nodes.label: Dams and pools
nodes.full: Hittite engineers built dams and holding pools to store water for cities and for the gods, as at Hattusa's Upper City and in Çorum's hills. At Eflatun Pınar, a spring sanctuary on a lake shore in the south, a carved facade of seated gods rises from the water. Water was part of the state cult.
nodes.src: Hittite water works (Seeher; Kohlmeyer); Eflatun Pınar studies by John Bean and Mark Weeden.

nodes.label: Hieroglyphic Luwian
nodes.full: Alongside the cuneiform of the archive, the court used an Anatolian hieroglyphic script, developed from seals for the Luwian language, for royal names and monuments. The Nişantaş and Yalburt inscriptions of the last kings are its monuments. After the empire, it persisted for centuries in the Neo-Hittite states.
nodes.src: J. David Hawkins, Corpus of Hieroglyphic Luwian Inscriptions (2000); Nişantaş and Yalburt inscriptions.

nodes.label: Iron
nodes.full: A letter by Hattusili III to a king explains that good iron cannot be had now in Kizzuwatna, promises to send a dagger blade and asks for patience. Iron objects were made as luxuries in small numbers. The old picture of a Hittite iron monopoly is a myth: the Iron Age came after the empire.
nodes.src: Letter KBo 1.14; Jane Waldbaum, From Bronze to Iron (1978).

nodes.label: Treaty with Egypt
nodes.full: Fifteen years after Kadesh, Hattusili III and Ramesses II made a treaty of peace and alliance, written in Akkadian and inscribed on silver tablets exchanged by envoys, with the gods of both lands as witnesses. Its Egyptian copy was carved at Karnak, and the Hittite copy was found at Hattusa. It is among the oldest surviving international peace treaties.
nodes.src: Treaty of Hattusili III and Ramesses II (CTH 91), Karnak and Ramesseum copies; Beckman 1996.

nodes.label: Egyptian queen’s letter
nodes.full: The widowed queen of Egypt, whom the Hittite text calls Dahamunzu, wrote to Suppiluliuma that her husband had died and that she had no son, and asked for one of his sons as husband. Suppiluliuma, who suspected a trap, sent an envoy and then a prince, Zannanza, who died on the way. The queen is usually identified as Ankhesenamun, widow of Tutankhamun.
nodes.src: Deeds of Suppiluliuma (CTH 40, fragment 28); Mursili II's Plague Prayers (CTH 378).

nodes.label: Great Kings’ brotherhood
nodes.full: Hattusa joined the diplomatic club of the great powers: letters addressed 'my brother, Great King' passed between Hatti, Egypt, Babylon, Assyria and Mitanni, with marriages, gift lists and complaints about the quality of gold. A Babylonian text of Kadashman-Enlil, a Kassite king, and Hattusili's replies bear witness to the rivalry for status.
nodes.src: Amarna letter EA 41 (Suppiluliuma to Akhenaten); the Hattusa correspondence (CTH 172–176); Beckman 1996.

nodes.label: Ahhiyawa
nodes.full: In the Tawagalawa letter a Hittite king writes to the king of Ahhiyawa as an equal and complains about the freebooter Piyamaradu, who had raided from Millawanda. Ahhiyawa is widely taken to be a Mycenaean-Greek state, Millawanda to be Miletus. In the Treaty with Shaushgamuwa the name of Ahhiyawa was struck from the list of kings of equal rank.
nodes.src: Tawagalawa letter (CTH 181); Milawata letter (CTH 182); Treaty with Shaushgamuwa of Amurru (CTH 105).

nodes.label: Wilusa
nodes.full: Muwatalli II made a treaty with Alaksandu, king of Wilusa, a western vassal whose land is usually identified with Troy, and whose name looks like Alexandros. The treaty ties Wilusa to the Great King's protection and lists its gods, among them a deity Appaliunas whom some read as an early form of Apollo. It is the main reason a late Bronze Age Troy matters to the Homeric question.
nodes.src: Treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa (CTH 76); Manapa-Tarhunta letter (CTH 191); Latacz, Troy and Homer (2004).

nodes.label: Uluburun ship
nodes.full: A ship that sank off Uluburun on the Lycian coast carried ten tons of copper ingots, a ton of tin, glass ingots, ivory, ebony and Canaanite jars. It was probably a Levantine ship, and its cargo reflects the kings' gift-exchange as well as trade. It is the best picture of the maritime world the Hittites faced across their south coast.
nodes.src: George Bass and Cemal Pulak, Uluburun excavation reports (1984–1994); Pulak 2008.

nodes.label: End of Mitanni
nodes.full: Mitanni, a large Hurrian state in northern Syria and Mesopotamia, was broken by Suppiluliuma and then eaten up by Assyria under Adad-nirari I. The Hittite king, who had set up a puppet state, found an Assyrian neighbour on the Euphrates in its place. The Late Bronze Age system of great powers lost Mitanni and gained Assyria.
nodes.src: Treaty with Shattiwaza (CTH 51); Assyrian royal inscriptions of Adad-nirari I.

nodes.label: The plague
nodes.full: Mursili's prayers say that the plague came with Egyptian prisoners taken in a raid on Amqa, and spread through the Hittite lands for twenty years, killing Suppiluliuma and his heir Arnuwanda II. The pestilence is thought to have reduced the army's manpower and the harvest. It is among the first epidemics for which a source names the route of contagion.
nodes.src: Plague Prayers of Mursili II (CTH 378); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: Drought
nodes.full: Tree rings in Gordion's juniper timbers show three years of exceptionally poor growth in 1198–1196 BC, within a drying trend of the thirteenth and twelfth centuries. The authors link it to food shortages in the landlocked heartland, as one pressure alongside others. The data come from a tomb built centuries later, and the link to the collapse is a correlation.
nodes.src: Sturt Manning et al., 'Severe multi-year drought coincident with Hittite collapse around 1198–1196 BC', Nature 614 (2023).

nodes.label: Bronze Age collapse
nodes.full: Within a generation Hattusa was abandoned, Ugarit was burned, Alashiya was attacked and Egypt fought the Sea Peoples. Ramesses III's Medinet Habu inscription says that no land could stand before them, from Hatti, Kode, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya onward. The Hittite state was one casualty of a regional breakdown whose causes were many.
nodes.src: Medinet Habu inscription of Ramesses III (c. 1177 BC); Eric Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014).

nodes.label: Kaska borderland
nodes.full: North of the heartland lived peoples without kings — the Kaska — who held the hills, raided into the plain and were never conquered, and who in the last years may have moved into the heartland. Hittite treaties with their chieftains were short-lived. They were the longest-lasting enemy of Hatti, the northern enemy of the state's own telling.
nodes.src: Prayer of Arnuwanda and Asmunikal (CTH 375); Bryce 1998; Trevor Bryce, The World of the Neo-Hittite Kingdoms (2012).

nodes.label: Puduhepa
nodes.full: Puduhepa, who was the daughter of a priest of Ishtar, married Hattusili III and became more than a consort. She had her own seal and used it on state documents, corresponded with Ramesses II and his queen Nefertari, helped to write the treaty and organised the cult. Her prayer to the Sun Goddess of Arinna shows her as a religious reformer.
nodes.src: Letters of Puduhepa to Ramesses II (CTH 176–177); Treaty with Egypt (CTH 91); Puduhepa's prayer (CTH 384).

nodes.label: Exiled Tawananna
nodes.full: Mursili II found his stepmother, Suppiluliuma's second wife, still sitting as tawananna, the queen with her own household. He charged her with causing the death of his wife through sorcery, and in a trial before the assembly stripped her of her office and exiled her.
nodes.src: Mursili II's Tawananna Tablet (CTH 70); Plague Prayers (CTH 378); Bryce 1998.

nodes.label: The deported
nodes.full: The deportees from conquered lands, the NAM.RA, were assigned to temples and palaces as labourers, farmers and craftsmen, and their legal status is given in the Hittite Laws. Tens of thousands were moved. We know of them only by the tallies of the conquerors.
nodes.src: Hittite Laws; Annals of Mursili II (CTH 61); Hoffner 1997.

nodes.label: Sickly boy
nodes.full: In his Apology, Hattusili tells that he was a weak child, so frail he was not expected to live, and that Ishtar of Samuha, the goddess who would protect him, was given to him in this way. He turned an old man's illness into proof of divine favour. It is an early text in which a ruler writes about his own sickness.
nodes.src: Apology of Hattusili III (CTH 81), §§2–3.

nodes.label: Death of Tutankhamun
nodes.full: Tutankhamun died around 1323 BC leaving no heir, which put his widow in the position of seeking a husband and brought the request to the Hittite king.
nodes.src: background — see the New Kingdom 1550–1200 BC folio (egypt-1550bc-1200bc)

nodes.label: Assyria under Adad-nirari, Shalmaneser and Tukulti-Ninurta
nodes.full: Assyria recovered from Mitanni’s domination, absorbed Mitanni’s eastern lands and grew into a rival on the Euphrates by the thirteenth century BC.
nodes.src: background — see the Middle Assyrian Kingdom 1400–1050 BC folio (assyria-1400bc-1050bc)

nodes.label: The Sea Peoples’ wars
nodes.full: Groups known to Egypt as the Sea Peoples attacked coasts and cities of the eastern Mediterranean around 1200–1177 BC, a part of the regional breakdown.
nodes.src: background — see the Third Intermediate Period folio (egypt-1200bc-664bc) and the Ugarit entries in the Canaan folio
